notes.10:10: Latin ut juvenes, et nutriti cum eo in deliciis ("as young men, and brought up with him in luxury") is a distinctly Vulgate expansion characterizing Rehoboam's young advisers.
notes.10:16: Latin rege duriora dicente ("as the king spoke harsher things") diverges from the Hebrew ("saw that the king did not listen to them"), and pasce ("shepherd") takes the Hebrew verb in its pastoral sense rather than "look to."
notes.10:18: Latin Aduram reflects the name form Adoram (as in 1 Kings 12:18) rather than the Hebrew spelling Hadoram in 2 Chronicles 10:18.
notes.11:4: The Vulgate reads "by My will" (mea ... voluntate), specifying divine agency where the Hebrew says simply "from Me."
notes.11:15: The Vulgate translates the Hebrew term for goat-idols or satyrs (se'irim) as "demons" (daemoniorum).
notes.11:18: The Vulgate puts "Abihail the daughter of Eliab" in the accusative case (Abihail quoque filiam), presenting Abihail as an additional wife of Rehoboam rather than as the mother of Mahalath.
notes.11:23: A distinctly Vulgate reading: the Latin presents this verse as explaining why Rehoboam chose Abijah ("because he was wiser and more powerful over all his sons"), whereas the Hebrew describes Rehoboam acting wisely by dispersing his sons across the fortified cities of Judah and Benjamin.
notes.12:3: Following the Septuagint, the Vulgate renders the Hebrew Sukkiim as "Troglodytes" (Troglodytae, cave-dwellers) and the Cushites as "Ethiopians" (Aethiopes).
notes.12:7: The Vulgate uses the vivid verb "drip" (stillabit) for God's wrath, where the Hebrew has "be poured out."
notes.12:9: A notable Vulgate-distinct reading: the Latin states that Shishak "withdrew from Jerusalem" (Recessit ... ab Jerusalem), following the narrative progression after 12:4, whereas the Hebrew reads "came up against Jerusalem."
notes.12:12: The Vulgate uses plural forms ("because they humbled themselves ... from them ... they were not completely destroyed") referring to king and people together, where the Hebrew uses the singular for Rehoboam, and renders Hebrew "good things" as "good works" (opera bona).
notes.12:15: The Vulgate translates the Hebrew phrase for genealogical enrollment as "carefully set forth" (diligenter exposita).
notes.13:4: Following the Septuagint, the Vulgate names this mountain "Mount Semeron" (montem Semeron), where the Hebrew reads "Mount Zemaraim."
notes.13:10: The Vulgate word order reads "our Lord is God" (Noster autem Dominus, Deus est) and uses the present tense "we do not abandon" (relinquimus), contrasting with the perfect "you have abandoned" (reliquistis) in 13:11.
notes.13:17: The Vulgate translates the Hebrew term for battle casualties (chalalim) literally as "wounded" (vulnerati).
notes.13:19: The Vulgate retains the Hebrew idiom "daughters" (filias) to designate the dependent villages and surrounding settlements belonging to each city.
notes.13:22: Where the Hebrew refers to the "midrash" or story of Iddo the prophet, the Vulgate renders "most carefully in the book of Iddo the prophet" (diligentissime in libro Addo prophetae).
notes.14:1: In the Clementine Vulgate, chapter 14 begins at verse 2 of the Hebrew and modern English numbering (since Hebrew 14:1 stands at Vulgate 13:23). The Vulgate also reads 'his God' (Dei sui) and 'altars of foreign worship' (altaria peregrini cultus).
notes.14:10: The Vulgate reads 'whether You assist with few or with many' (utrum in paucis auxilieris, an in pluribus), whereas the Hebrew reads 'between the mighty and the one who has no strength.'
notes.14:11: The Vulgate reads 'terrified' (Exterruit, echoing the 'great terror' of 14:13, where Latin omits 'of the Lord'), whereas the Hebrew reads 'struck down' or 'defeated.'
notes.15:4: In 15:3-6, the Vulgate exhibits a distinctive sequence of tenses—imperfect 'passed' (Transibant, 15:3), future 'will find' and 'will be' (reperient, erit, 15:4-5), and perfect 'has fought' paired with future 'will throw them into turmoil' (pugnavit, conturbabit, 15:6)—treating part of Azariah's speech prophetically where the Hebrew looks back historically.
notes.15:8: The Vulgate explicitly reads 'Azariah the son of Oded the prophet' (Azariæ filii Oded prophetæ), whereas the Hebrew omits 'Azariah the son of'; Latin also reads 'dedicated' (dedicavit) rather than Hebrew 'repaired' or 'renewed.'
notes.15:12: The Vulgate uses a singular verb referring to Asa and includes 'according to custom' (intravit ex more), whereas the Hebrew uses a plural verb ('they entered into a covenant') without that phrase.
notes.15:15: Instead of the Hebrew 'all Judah rejoiced over the oath,' the Vulgate links 'all who were in Judah' to 'swore' in 15:14 and specifies 'with a curse' (cum execratione), indicating a solemn self-imprecatory oath.
notes.15:16: Jerome renders the Hebrew office of queen mother with the Roman imperial phrase 'august authority' (augusto imperio) and interprets Maacah's abominable Asherah image as a statue of the classical fertility god Priapus (simulacrum Priapi). The Clementine spelling 'in frustra' stands for 'in frusta' ('into pieces').
notes.16:4: The Vulgate specifies 'walled cities' (urbes muratas), whereas the Hebrew reads 'store cities.'
notes.16:9: The Vulgate states that the Lord's eyes 'survey' (contemplantur) the whole earth and provide strength to those who 'believe in Him' (credunt in eum), where the Hebrew speaks of His eyes ranging throughout the earth to support those whose heart is wholly His.
notes.16:10: The Vulgate states that Asa 'killed very many' (interfecit plurimos) of the people, whereas the Hebrew reads that he oppressed or crushed some of them.
notes.16:14: The Vulgate renders Hebrew zenim ('various kinds [of spices]') via the similar root for harlotry as 'prostitutes' ointments' (unguentibus meretriciis), and describes the great funeral fire as burning them over him 'with excessive pomp' (ambitione nimia).
notes.17:3: Vulgate "did not hope" (non speravit) renders the Hebrew verb meaning "sought"; similarly in v. 4 Vulgate has "sins" (peccata) where the Hebrew has "deeds" or "practices."
notes.17:6: Vulgate "groves" (lucos) regularly translates the Hebrew Asherim (sacred wooden poles or cultic groves associated with Asherah), as also in 19:3.
notes.17:12: Vulgate "houses like towers and walled cities" (domos ad instar turrium, urbesque muratas) differs from the Hebrew, which refers to fortresses and store cities.
notes.17:17: The Clementine Vulgate omits the tribal designation "of Benjamin" found in the Hebrew at the opening of this verse.
notes.18:10: Vulgate "toss" (ventilabis, literally "winnow" or "toss into the air") vividly renders the Hebrew verb meaning "gore" with horns.
notes.18:15: Vulgate "Again and again I adjure you" (Iterum atque iterum te adjuro) renders the Hebrew rhetorical question ("How many times must I make you swear?") as a solemn statement.
notes.18:25: Vulgate "son of Amelech" (filium Amelech) transliterates the Hebrew title hammelekh ("the king," i.e., "the king's son") as a personal name. In v. 26, Vulgate "a little bread and a very little water" renders the Hebrew "bread of affliction and water of affliction" as meager rations.
notes.18:30: Vulgate "cavalry" (equitatus) translates the Hebrew term for "chariots" throughout vv. 30-32.
notes.18:33: Vulgate "between the neck and the shoulder blades" (inter cervicem et scapulas) differs from the Hebrew "between the joints and the breastplate"; likewise in v. 34, Vulgate "the battle came to an end" (finita est pugna) contrasts with the Hebrew "the battle grew fierce."
notes.19:2: Vulgate states the rebuke declaratively ("You offer help... you indeed deserved the wrath of the Lord") rather than as a question as in the Hebrew, and in v. 3 expands Hebrew "God" to "the Lord God of your fathers."
notes.19:6: Vulgate "whatever you judge will come back upon you" (quodcumque judicaveritis, in vos redundabit) differs notably from the Hebrew "He is with you in the matter of judgment."
notes.19:10: Vulgate "between kindred and kindred" (inter cognationem et cognationem) interprets the Hebrew phrase "between blood and blood" (cases of bloodshed) in terms of blood kinship.
notes.19:11: Vulgate "in good things" (in bonis) renders the Hebrew "with the good," which can be understood either of upright persons or of good deeds.
notes.20:1: Vulgate reads "some of the Ammonites" (de Ammonitis), reflecting the consonantal Hebrew text; many modern translations emend this to "Meunites" based on the Septuagint.
notes.20:7: Vulgate reads "put to death" (interfecisti) where the Hebrew Masoretic Text reads "drove out."
notes.20:21: Vulgate reads "gave counsel to the people" (deditque consilium populo) and "in their companies" (in turmis suis), whereas the Hebrew Masoretic Text has "took counsel with the people" and "in holy splendor."
notes.20:22: Vulgate specifies that the Lord turned the enemies' own ambushes against themselves (vertit Dominus insidias eorum in semetipsos), whereas the Hebrew text speaks of the Lord setting ambushers against them.
notes.20:26: Vulgate translates the Hebrew place name Beracah literally into Latin as Vallis benedictionis ("Valley of Blessing").
notes.21:2: Vulgate reads "king of Judah" (regis Juda), whereas the Hebrew Masoretic Text reads "king of Israel."
notes.21:3: Vulgate renders the Hebrew term for precious gifts or valuables as pensitationes ("revenues" or "payments").
notes.21:9: Vulgate reads "cavalry" (equitatu) twice here where the Hebrew Masoretic Text reads "chariots."
notes.21:11: Vulgate reads "in the cities of Judah" (in urbibus Juda), agreeing with the Septuagint against the Hebrew Masoretic Text's "in the hill country of Judah."
notes.21:20: Vulgate interprets the Hebrew clause "he departed with no one's regret" morally as Ambulavitque non recte ("And he did not walk rightly").
notes.22:2: Vulgate preserves "forty-two" (quadraginta duorum) in agreement with the Hebrew Masoretic Text here, in contrast to "twenty-two" in 2 Kings 8:26 and the Septuagint.
notes.22:6: Vulgate summarizes the Hebrew reference to the battle at Ramah as "in the aforementioned battle" (in supradicto certamine), and reads "Ahaziah" (Ochozias) where the Hebrew Masoretic Text has the variant "Azariah."
notes.22:7: Vulgate reads "it was the will of God" (Voluntatis quippe fuit Dei), whereas the Hebrew Masoretic Text reads "the downfall of Ahaziah was from God."
notes.22:9: Vulgate renders the final clause as "there was no longer any hope" (Nec erat ultra spes aliqua), whereas the Hebrew text states that the house of Ahaziah had no one able to retain strength for the kingdom.
notes.22:10: Vulgate reads "of the house of Jehoram" (domus Joram), whereas the Hebrew Masoretic Text reads "of the house of Judah."
notes.23:5: Unlike the Hebrew verse division (which places the first third in v. 4 as gatekeepers of the thresholds), the Vulgate moves all three divisions into v. 5 and coordinates 'of the gatekeepers' (et janitorum) with the priests and Levites stationed at the gates.
notes.23:11: Alongside placing the diadem and the testimony on the king, the Vulgate adds the explanatory clause 'and gave the law into his hand to hold' (dederuntque in manu ejus tenendam legem), as well as 'and they invoked blessings upon him' (imprecatique sunt ei) before the acclamation.
notes.23:13: Where the Hebrew describes the king standing by his pillar with the captains and trumpeters, the Vulgate reads 'upon the step' (super gradum) and 'the leaders and the companies around him' (et principes, turmasque circa eum).
notes.23:14: Whereas the Hebrew has Jehoiada bring out the commanders and order Athaliah led between the ranks (with any follower killed), the Vulgate has him go out to the centurions and army leaders and order her brought 'beyond the precincts of the temple' (extra septa templi) to be put to death outside.
notes.24:13: The Vulgate renders the Hebrew healing metaphor for temple repair vividly as 'the scar of the walls was closed over by their hands' (obducebatur parietum cicatrix per manus eorum).
notes.24:16: Unlike the Hebrew ('toward God and His house'), the Vulgate omits 'God' here, reading simply 'toward Israel and toward his house' (cum Israel, et cum domo ejus).
notes.24:20: By placing 'the priest' (sacerdotem) in the accusative, the Vulgate explicitly applies the priestly title to Zechariah himself; it also reads 'in the sight of the people' (in conspectu populi) rather than 'above the people' and 'the Lord God' (Dominus Deus) rather than 'God'.
notes.24:25: The Vulgate reads singular 'the son of Jehoiada the priest' (filii Jojadae sacerdotis), matching vv. 20-22, where the Masoretic Hebrew has the plural 'sons'.
notes.24:27: Rendering the Hebrew term for 'burden/oracle' in a financial sense and 'commentary' adverbially, the Vulgate speaks of 'the sum of money that had been gathered together under him' (summa pecuniae quae adunata fuerat sub eo) and states that these matters 'are written more carefully in the book of the kings' (scripta sunt diligentius in libro regum).
notes.25:8: The Vulgate translates the difficult Hebrew clause as a clear conditional statement ("if you think that wars depend on the strength of an army"), whereas the Masoretic Hebrew is usually rendered "if you go, act, be strong for battle."
notes.25:17: The Vulgate explicitly adds the judgment "very bad" (pessimo) to Amaziah's counsel, whereas the Masoretic Hebrew simply states that he "took counsel."
notes.25:24: Latin filios obsidum ("sons of the hostages") is a literal rendering of the Hebrew idiom for hostages ("sons of pledges").
notes.25:28: The Vulgate reads "in the city of David" (agreeing with 2 Kings 14:20 and some ancient witnesses), whereas the Masoretic Hebrew reads "in the city of Judah."
notes.26:5: Latin intelligentis et videntis Deum literally reads "who understood and saw God," where the Masoretic Hebrew is commonly rendered "who instructed him in the fear of God" (or "in visions of God").
notes.26:7: The Vulgate reads "against the Ammonites" (matching 26:8), whereas the Masoretic Hebrew reads "against the Meunites."
notes.26:8: The Vulgate reads "because of his frequent victories" (propter crebras victorias), where the Masoretic Hebrew reads "for he became exceedingly strong."
notes.26:11: Latin doctoris ("teacher" or "instructor") is Jerome's rendering of the Hebrew title for an administrative official (shoter).
notes.26:18: Latin ne contempseris gives a negative command ("do not show contempt"), whereas the Masoretic Hebrew gives a statement ("for you have acted unfaithfully").
notes.27:7: The Vulgate reads "and works" (et opera), whereas the Masoretic Hebrew reads "and his ways."
notes.27:9: The Clementine Vulgate moves directly from 27:7 to 27:9, omitting the duplicate summary of Jotham's age and length of reign numbered 27:8 in the Masoretic Hebrew (already stated in 27:1).
notes.28:3: Latin lustravit ("purified") denotes ritual purification by fire, and interfecit ... in adventu reads "killed ... at the arrival," whereas the Hebrew Masoretic Text reads "burned" and "drove out before."
notes.28:10: Latin quod nequaquam facto opus est ("which by no means needs to be done") is a distinctly Vulgate statement, whereas the Hebrew Masoretic Text asks rhetorically whether Israel does not also have sins against the Lord.
notes.28:15: Latin quos supra memoravimus ("whom we mentioned above") renders Hebrew "who were designated by name," and propter laborem, et adhibuissent eis curam ("because of their weariness, and given them care") is a Vulgate explanatory expansion.
notes.28:19: Latin regem Juda ("king of Judah") and nudasset eum auxilio ("stripped it of help") are Vulgate-distinct readings where the Hebrew Masoretic Text reads "king of Israel" and "cast off restraint in Judah."
notes.28:20: Latin Adduxitque makes the Lord (from v. 19) the subject who brought Tiglath-pileser (Latin Thelgathphalnasar) against Ahaz, and nullo resistente vastavit ("devastated him with no one resisting") differs from the Hebrew "did not strengthen him."
notes.29:13: Latin reads Jahiel ("Jehiel") in both vv. 13 and 14, whereas the Hebrew Masoretic Text reads "Jeuel" (or "Jeiel") in v. 13 and "Jehiel" in v. 14; similarly in v. 12 Latin Gersom ("Gershom") corresponds to Hebrew "Gershon."
notes.29:19: Latin polluerat ("had defiled") differs from the Hebrew Masoretic Text, which reads "had cast aside" (or "rejected").
notes.29:31: "You have filled your hands" renders the literal Latin idiom Implestis manus vestras, denoting consecration to the service of the Lord.
notes.29:34: Latin faciliori ritu sanctificantur ("are sanctified by an easier rite") is a well-known Vulgate-distinct reading; the Hebrew Masoretic Text reads "were more upright in heart to sanctify themselves."
notes.29:36: Latin eo quod ministerium Domini esset expletum: de repente quippe hoc fieri placuerat ("because the service of the Lord had been fulfilled; for indeed it had seemed good for this to happen suddenly") differs from the Hebrew "over what God had prepared for the people, because the thing came about suddenly."
notes.30:11: Vulgate 'consenting to the counsel' (acquiescentes consilio), where the Hebrew Masoretic Text reads 'humbled themselves'.
notes.30:15: Vulgate 'at last sanctified' (tandem sanctificati), whereas the Hebrew Masoretic Text reads 'were put to shame and sanctified themselves'.
notes.30:19: Vulgate explicitly states 'and will not count it against them that they were insufficiently sanctified' (et non imputabit eis quod minus sanctificati sunt), expanding the briefer Hebrew clause 'though not according to the purification of the sanctuary'.
notes.30:20: Vulgate 'was appeased toward the people' (placatus est populo), where the Hebrew Masoretic Text reads 'healed the people'.
notes.31:1: Vulgate 'groves' (lucos) is Jerome's standard Latin rendering of the Hebrew Asherah poles (asherim), and 'images' (simulacra) corresponds to the Hebrew sacred pillars.
notes.31:3: Vulgate 'first days of the months' renders Latin calendis (Kalends, corresponding to the new-moon observances), and reads 'in the law of Moses' (in lege Moysi) where the Hebrew Masoretic Text has 'in the law of the Lord'.
notes.31:13: Vulgate reads 'Azariah' (Azarias) for the second supervisor, whereas the Hebrew Masoretic Text reads 'Azaziah'; the final clause 'to whom all things pertained' (ad quos omnia pertinebant) is a Vulgate explanatory addition.
notes.31:15: Vulgate reads 'Benjamin' (Benjamin), whereas the Hebrew Masoretic Text reads 'Miniamin'.
notes.31:20: Vulgate 'all the things that we have said' (universa quae diximus) introduces a first-person-plural narratorial phrase not present in the Hebrew Masoretic Text ('thus Hezekiah did').
notes.32:1: Vulgate 'hujuscemodi veritatem' literally reads "truthfulness of this sort" (rendering Hebrew 'emet', faithfulness/truth), and 'rex Assyriorum' reads "king of the Assyrians" rather than "king of Assyria."
notes.32:18: Unlike the Hebrew plural ("they cried out... to frighten... and capture"), the Vulgate uses singular verbs ('personabat', 'terreret', 'caperet', continuing in 32:19 'Locutusque est'), attributing the proclamation directly to Sennacherib or his spokesman.
notes.32:20: The Vulgate spells Isaiah's father's name as 'Amos' (identical to the prophet Amos), whereas standard English distinguishes him as Amoz following the Hebrew.
notes.32:22: Vulgate 'præstitit eis quietem per circuitum' ("granted them rest on every side") follows the Septuagint reading rather than the Hebrew Masoretic Text's "guided them on every side."
notes.32:33: Vulgate 'celebravit ejus exequias' ("celebrated his funeral rites") specifies funeral ceremonies, whereas the Hebrew reads more generally "did him honor at his death."
notes.33:3: Vulgate 'lucos' ("sacred groves") renders the Hebrew 'asherim' (sacred poles or Asherah images), a characteristic Vulgate rendering also used in 33:19.
notes.33:6: Vulgate 'observabat somnia' ("observed dreams") interprets the Hebrew divination verb as dream-omen observation.
notes.33:11: Vulgate 'catenis atque compedibus' ("in chains and shackles") renders the Hebrew "with hooks and bronze fetters" without the specific reference to hooks.
notes.33:12: Vulgate 'egit pœnitentiam' ("did penance," repeated in 33:19) renders the Hebrew verb meaning "humbled himself."
notes.33:23: Vulgate 'non est reveritus faciem Domini' ("did not show reverence before the face of the Lord") differs from the Hebrew, which states that Amon "did not humble himself before the Lord."
notes.34:3: Latin "lucis" ("sacred groves") is the Vulgate's regular rendering of the Hebrew Asherah poles, and in 34:4 "simulacra quae superposita fuerant" ("statues that had been set upon them") corresponds to the incense altars of the Hebrew text.
notes.34:9: Vulgate "acceptamque ab eo pecuniam" ("having received from him the money") depicts the envoys receiving the money from Hilkiah to hand over to the overseers in 34:10, whereas the Hebrew text says they delivered the money to Hilkiah.
notes.34:21: Latin "orate Dominum" ("pray to the Lord") replaces the Hebrew "inquire of the Lord," and "stillavit" (also in 34:25) literally means "dripped" or "dropped down," picturing divine wrath pouring down from above.
notes.34:22: Latin "in Secunda" (literally "in the Second") refers to the Second District or Quarter of Jerusalem, and the closing clause "verba quae supra narravimus" ("the words that we have recounted above") is a distinctive Vulgate narrator's remark where the Hebrew simply has "to this effect."
notes.34:31: Latin "in tribunali suo" ("on his platform," literally "on his tribunal") renders the Hebrew "in his place" or "by his pillar," depicting a raised royal stand; in 34:32 "Adjuravit" ("placed under oath") renders the Hebrew "made to stand."
notes.35:3: Latin "ad quorum eruditionem omnis Israel sanctificabatur Domino" ("by whose instruction all Israel was sanctified to the Lord") makes all Israel the passive subject of sanctification, whereas the Hebrew text describes the Levites themselves as teachers of Israel who were holy to the Lord.
notes.35:15: Latin "prophetarum regis" ("the prophets of the king") is plural in the Vulgate, applying to Asaph, Heman, and Jeduthun together, whereas the Hebrew singular ("the king's seer") modifies Jeduthun alone.
notes.35:18: The Vulgate places "sacerdotibus ... omni Judae ... et habitantibus" in the dative case ("for the priests ... all Judah ... and those living in Jerusalem"), presenting Josiah as keeping the Passover on their behalf rather than coordinating them as co-subjects with Josiah as in the Hebrew.
notes.35:22: Vulgate "praeparavit contra eum bellum" ("prepared war against him") differs from the Hebrew Masoretic Text, which states that Josiah disguised himself to fight Necho.
notes.35:25: Latin "Jeremias maxime" ("Jeremiah most of all") continues the verb "mourned" from 35:24, and "Ecce scriptum fertur in lamentationibus" ("Look, it is said to be written in the Lamentations") uses "fertur" ("is reported" or "handed down") where the Hebrew simply states that they are written in the laments.
notes.36:6: The Vulgate reads "king of the Chaldeans" (Latin rex Chaldaeorum) where the Hebrew has "king of Babylon," and uses the indicative "led him... into Babylon" (duxit in Babylonem) where the Hebrew expresses purpose ("to take him to Babylon").
notes.36:10: The Vulgate reads "his uncle" (Latin patruum ejus, paternal uncle, agreeing with 2 Kings 24:17) where the Hebrew text of 2 Chronicles has "his brother."
notes.36:12: The Vulgate reads "was not ashamed before the face of Jeremiah" (Latin nec erubuit faciem Jeremiae), whereas the Hebrew text reads "did not humble himself before Jeremiah."
notes.36:15: The Vulgate reads "rising up in the night and warning them daily" (Latin de nocte consurgens, et quotidie commonens), rendering the Hebrew idiom for persistent sending with the imagery of rising before dawn and admonishing every day.
notes.36:17: The Vulgate keeps a continuous third-person singular subject across the verse, reading "in the house of His sanctuary" (in domo sanctuarii sui, reflexive to the Lord) and connecting "had no compassion" directly to "handed them all over into his hands" with "but" (sed). The Hebrew instead reads "their sanctuary" and is commonly read with the Chaldean king as the subject of the killing.
